title: Writer's Goal: Choosing Content That Meets a Purpose
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · English: Organisation, Relevance and Style
summary: How to answer "Which choice most effectively…" and "Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been…" questions by matching the exact goal words and judging what the essay really does.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Writer's-goal questions belong to **Production of Writing**, the reporting category that is 38–43% of the ACT English score. They test whether you can choose the content that does a **stated job**. The stem tells you the job; your task is to find the one choice that does exactly that job — not the one that is simply true, correct or attractive.
They come in two main forms:

rows: Goal for one part
"The writer wants to emphasise / show / give a specific example of … Which choice best accomplishes this goal?" or simply "Which choice most effectively …?"
On an underlined word, phrase or sentence anywhere in the essay
Goal for the whole essay
"Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to … Would this essay accomplish that purpose?"
Usually the last question of an essay

blocks.text: In the first form, all four choices are usually grammatical and on the general topic. Three of them do a slightly different job. In the second form, two choices say Yes and two say No, each with a reason; you must judge the essay and then the reason.

blocks.title: اقرا المطلوب بالظبط
blocks.text: في أسئلة Which choice most effectively… كل الاختيارات جمل سليمة. علّم على الكلمات اللي بتقول الهدف (specific / emphasise / picture / contrast / introduce / conclude) واسأل عن كل اختيار: هو بيعمل الهدف ده بالظبط؟ مش: هو جملة حلوة؟
The method for "Which choice most effectively …"

items: **Underline the goal words** in the stem, for example: "specific sense of HOW MANY," "emphasise how HARD," "show TRUST in the writer's skill."
**Split two-part goals.** "Admit the changes AND show the market feels the same" needs both halves. A choice that does only one half is wrong.
**Test every choice against the goal words only.** Ask "Does this show trust?" — not "Is this true? Is this a good sentence?"
**Look for the exact focus.** A choice can match the topic but miss the job: liking the shop is not trusting the writer; a long trip is not a hard trip.
**Read the sentence before and after.** The right choice must also fit the paragraph; if it contradicts the next sentence, it is wrong.

blocks.text: Goal words and what the right choice contains

rows: most specific / most detailed / most precise
has names, numbers, exact places, concrete actions
vague words: many, some, various, a lot, near, things
help the reader picture / visualise
gives a concrete image, often a comparison or sensory detail
states the idea in abstract words ("it was small")
emphasise [a quality]
shows that exact quality with evidence
shows a near-quality (long ≠ hard; popular ≠ trusted)
show a contrast with what came before
contains an opposite idea
adds a new idea in the same direction
give an example / illustrate
gives one concrete case of the claim
repeats the claim in general words
introduce the paragraph / the essay
names the topic the next sentences develop
too broad, too narrow, or off-topic
conclude / return to the opening
closes the main idea, often echoing the first paragraph
a new topic or a small new detail
be most relevant to the paragraph's focus
links directly to what the paragraph is about
true facts about something nearby

blocks.text: Choosing the detail that meets a stated purpose
Most goal questions are about **details**. Think of the goal as a filter: let through only the detail that serves it.

items: Goal: show how **dedicated** the volunteers were.
✓ volunteers, who did not miss a single week even during exams, (dedication: never missing)
✗ volunteers from several different grades (variety, not dedication)
Goal: give the most **specific** location of the collection point.
✓ beside the main gate, next to the guard's room (two exact landmarks)
✗ somewhere on the school grounds (vague)
Goal: show that the principal was persuaded **by the evidence**.
✓ After studying our chart of the week's totals, she agreed (links her decision to the data)
✗ She smiled warmly and agreed (kindness, not evidence)
Goal: emphasise how **hard** the journey was.
✓ men and animals sometimes went several days between wells
✗ The trip was long. (length, not hardship)

blocks.text: **Two-part goals** are where many strong students lose marks. If the stem says "to show both the size of the crowd and its mood," a choice with a number but no feeling, or a feeling but no number, is wrong.

items: Goal: show both the size of the crowd and its excitement.
✓ More than five thousand fans jumped and sang for the whole second half. (size + excitement)
✗ More than five thousand fans filled the stadium. (size only)
✗ The fans were thrilled. (excitement only)

blocks.title: الهدف اللي ليه جزئين
blocks.text: لو السؤال طالب حاجتين (both … and …)، لازم الاختيار يعمل الاتنين. اختيار بيعمل نص الهدف بس يبقى غلط حتى لو كلامه صح. ولو مطلوب specific دوّر على أرقام وأسماء وأماكن محددة، مش كلمات زي many أو some.
The method for "Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been …"

items: **Read the hypothetical purpose carefully.** Note the topic (bicycle repair, factory recycling) AND the kind of essay (explain steps, argue, compare, tell a personal story, give a history). Note the scope: one person's experience, or a general explanation?
**Say in one sentence what the essay really does,** for example: "A teenager tells how one summer in his uncle's shop taught him to work with his hands."

**Compare.** If the topic, the kind of essay and the scope all match, the answer is Yes. If any one differs, it is No. The word "primary" matters: a topic that appears in one paragraph is not the primary purpose.
**Choose the reason that describes the essay accurately.** Cross out reasons that are false about the essay, and reasons that treat a small detail as the main point.

rows: explain the steps of repairing a bicycle
a personal story about a summer in a repair shop
No — story, not a how-to explanation
describe a family member's craft in a personal essay
the writer describes her grandfather's carpentry workshop and the chair he made for her
Yes — personal and about his craft
argue that cities should build rooftop gardens
neighbours describe how they built one rooftop garden
No — a personal account, not an argument about cities
explain how paper is recycled in factories
a student council's paper-collection project at one school
No — a school project, not factory processes

blocks.text: On these questions, the right answer is often No, because the stated purpose is usually close to the essay but not the same. Do not guess No automatically, though: check the match each time.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — specific detail**
Passage: Wildlife officers on the Red Sea coast count the dugongs that feed on sea grass near the shore. __The animals are hard to see.__
**The writer wants to give a specific reason why counting the dugongs is difficult. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) The animals are shy and can stay underwater for several minutes at a time.
C) The dugong is a distant relative of the elephant.
D) Many tourists hope to see a dugong.

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: True but vague — it gives no specific reason.
B) ✓ Correct: Two specific reasons the animals are hard to count.
C) ✗ Wrong: An interesting fact, but about the animal's family, not about counting.
D) ✗ Wrong: Off-topic: tourists, not counting.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — emphasise a quality**
Passage: Every Thursday, __volunteers__ carried the full recycling boxes to the collection point.
**The writer wants to emphasise how dedicated the volunteers were. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) a group of volunteers
C) volunteers from several different grades
D) volunteers, who did not miss a single week even during exams,

blocks.text: **Answer: D**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Says nothing about dedication.
B) ✗ Wrong: Adds a word but no quality.
C) ✗ Wrong: A near-quality: variety, not dedication.
D) ✓ Correct: Never missing a week, even during exams, is proof of dedication.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — two-part goal**
Passage: After the final whistle, __the fans left the stadium.__
**The writer wants to show both how many fans there were and how happy they were. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) thousands of fans poured out of the stadium, singing and waving flags.
C) the fans were delighted.
D) more than forty thousand fans left the stadium.

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Neither part of the goal.
B) ✓ Correct: Both parts: thousands (number) + singing and waving flags (happiness).
C) ✗ Wrong: Happiness only — no number.
D) ✗ Wrong: Number only — no happiness.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — primary purpose**
Passage: (Imagine an essay in which a student describes her grandfather's carpentry workshop: the smell of wood, the tools on the wall, and the chair he built for her tenth birthday.)
**Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to write a personal essay about a family member's craft. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?**

items: A) Yes, because it describes the grandfather's workshop and a piece of furniture he made for the writer.
B) Yes, because it explains the history of carpentry in Egypt.
C) No, because it focuses on the writer's own hobby.
D) No, because it gives instructions for building a chair.

blocks.text: **Answer: A**

items: A) ✓ Correct: The essay is personal and is about the grandfather's craft — topic, kind and scope all match, and the reason is accurate.
B) ✗ Wrong: Right decision, false reason: the essay has no history of carpentry.
C) ✗ Wrong: False: the craft is the grandfather's, not the writer's.
D) ✗ Wrong: False: the essay describes a chair; it gives no instructions.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **True but not the job:** a correct, pleasant sentence that does a different job from the stated goal.
**Near-quality:** variety instead of dedication, liking instead of trust, long instead of hard.
**Vague choice for a "specific" goal:** many, some, various, a lot, near the gate.
**Half a two-part goal:** a choice that does only one of the two things asked.
**Opposite of the goal:** "My first patches were fine" when the goal is to show difficulty.
**Small detail as the main point** in "Suppose…" questions: one paragraph about patching tyres does not make a how-to essay.
**Right decision, wrong reason:** Yes/No is correct but the reason describes the essay falsely.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Underline the goal words before you read the choices.
Cross out every choice that does a different job, however good it sounds.
For "specific," look for numbers, names and exact places; for "picture," look for a concrete image.
For two-part goals, tick each part separately.
Answer "Suppose…" questions last, after summarising the whole essay in one sentence.

blocks.text: Practice
Read the two essays and answer the 10 questions. Each question states a goal; choose the option that meets it. Question 10 asks about the second essay as a whole.

blocks.title: Writer's goal — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two short essays, 10 questions on choosing content that meets a stated goal or purpose. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
Forty Days to Market

Every Friday morning, a wide, dusty field at Birqash, northwest of Cairo, fills with camels. [1] __Many animals are there.__ Traders shout prices, buyers check teeth and legs, and young herders keep the animals in line with long sticks. The air smells of hay, dust and diesel from the trucks parked along the road.

For centuries, most of these camels began their journey in Sudan. Herders walked them north along an ancient desert route known as the Forty Days Road. [2] __The trip was long.__

[3] __Today, modern transport has changed the way camels reach the market.__ Most now travel by truck for at least part of the way, and the journey takes days rather than weeks. Herders who once spent a month in the desert now ride in the cab beside the driver.

The buyers have changed less than the journey. Farmers still come to buy strong animals for work, and [4] __other people come too__. Prices are agreed with a handshake, and money changes hands in thick bundles of notes. By early afternoon, most of the camels have new owners. [5] __The market closes soon afterwards.__
questions.q: Question 1: The writer wants to give a specific sense of how many camels the market holds. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
c: NO CHANGE
Camels are large and strong animals.
On a busy day, more than a thousand camels may stand tied in rows across the field.
The animals come in many shades of brown.
questions.e: The goal words are "specific" and "how many." Only C gives a number and a picture (rows across the field). A is true but vague; B is about size and strength, not number; D is about colour.

questions.q: Question 2: The writer wants to emphasise how hard the journey along the Forty Days Road was. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
c: NO CHANGE
Water was scarce, and men and animals sometimes went several days between wells.
The route crossed part of Egypt's Western Desert.
Most of the herders were young men.
questions.e: B shows hardship with a concrete detail: days without water. A says only that it was long, not hard; C names the place without showing difficulty; D is about the herders' age.

questions.q: Question 3: Which choice most effectively introduces the main point of this paragraph?
c: NO CHANGE
Today, camels are still sold at the market.
Today, camel milk is popular in some countries.
Today, many visitors take photographs at the market.
questions.e: The paragraph is about how trucks have shortened the journey, and the underlined sentence names exactly that change. B says nothing has changed — the opposite of the paragraph's point; C and D are off-topic.

questions.q: Question 4: Which choice provides the most specific information about the other buyers who come to the market?
c: NO CHANGE
many different kinds of buyers attend
people arrive from various places
butchers from towns across the Delta come to buy camels for meat
questions.e: D says who (butchers), where from (towns across the Delta) and why (meat). A, B and C are all vague — "other people," "different kinds," "various places" give the reader nothing concrete.

questions.q: Question 5: The writer wants to conclude the essay by suggesting that, despite the changes, the market still feels much as it did in the past. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
c: NO CHANGE
Camels are well suited to life in the desert.
The roads are new, but every Friday the shouting, the dust and the long rows of camels look much as they must have looked a century ago.
Visitors should bring water and a hat.
questions.e: The goal has two parts: admit the changes AND show that the market feels the same. C does both ("The roads are new, but … look much as they must have looked a century ago") and echoes the opening scene. A only gives a closing time; B is a general fact; D is advice to tourists.

questions.p:
Learning to Fix Bicycles

The summer I turned fifteen, my uncle Sami let me work in his bicycle repair shop in Zagazig. [6] __The shop was small.__ Every wall was covered with hooks holding wheels, chains and inner tubes, and the air smelled of oil and rubber.

On my first day, my uncle gave me a simple job: patching flat tyres. I removed each tube, pumped air into it and held it under water to find the tiny stream of bubbles that showed the hole. [7] __My first patches were fine.__ My uncle watched, said nothing, and handed me another tube.

Slowly I learned more. By August, I could replace a chain, straighten a bent wheel and adjust brakes, and I no longer needed to ask my uncle for help with every job. [8] __Regular customers began to hand their bicycles straight to me instead of waiting for my uncle.__

On my last day, my uncle gave me a small screwdriver with my name scratched into its handle. "You earned this," he said. [9] __The handle was made of red plastic.__

[Question 10 asks about the essay as a whole.]
questions.q: Question 6: The writer wants to help the reader picture just how small the shop was. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
c: NO CHANGE
The shop was not large at all.
The shop was in an old building near the station.
The shop was so narrow that two customers could not stand side by side.
questions.e: "Picture" asks for a concrete image. D gives one: two customers could not stand side by side. A and B only state the idea; C is about age and location, not size.
questions.s: Writer's goal — help the reader picture

Learning to Fix Bicycles

On my first day, my uncle gave me a simple job: patching flat tyres. I removed each tube, pumped air into it and held it under water to find the tiny stream of bubbles that showed the hole. [7] __My first patches were fine.__ My uncle watched, said nothing, and handed me another tube.

Slowly I learned more. By August, I could replace a chain, straighten a bent wheel and adjust brakes, and I no longer needed to ask my uncle for help with every job. [8] __Regular customers began to hand their bicycles straight to me instead of waiting for my uncle.__

On my last day, my uncle gave me a small screwdriver with my name scratched into its handle. "You earned this," he said. [9] __The handle was made of red plastic.__

[Question 10 asks about the essay as a whole.]
questions.q: Question 7: Which choice most effectively shows that the writer found the work difficult at first?
c: NO CHANGE
My first three patches leaked within an hour, and I had to redo every one.
Patches come in several sizes.
My uncle sold each patch for two pounds.
questions.e: B shows difficulty with a concrete result: leaking patches that had to be redone — and it explains why the uncle silently handed over another tube. A says the opposite (the work went fine); C and D are facts about patches, not about the writer's struggle.

[Question 10 asks about the essay as a whole.]
questions.q: Question 8: The writer wants to show that customers had come to trust the writer's skill. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
c: NO CHANGE
Customers liked the shop very much.
Some customers came from other neighbourhoods.
The shop opened at eight every morning.
questions.e: Handing their bicycles to the writer instead of waiting for the uncle is proof of trust in the writer himself. B shows liking for the shop, not trust in the writer; C shows the shop's reach; D is a schedule detail.

[Question 10 asks about the essay as a whole.]
questions.q: Question 9: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by showing that the summer had a lasting importance for the writer?
c: NO CHANGE
I still use it whenever my own bicycle needs a repair, and each time I do, I remember the summer I learned to work with my hands.
Screwdrivers are among the most useful tools.
My uncle still runs the shop today.
questions.e: "Lasting importance for the writer" needs the present day AND the writer's feelings. B has both: he still uses the screwdriver and still remembers the summer. A describes the handle; C is a general fact; D is about the uncle, not the writer.

questions.q: Question 10: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain the steps involved in repairing a bicycle. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?
c: Yes, because it describes how the writer patched flat tyres.
Yes, because it lists several repairs the writer learned to do.
No, because it focuses on the writer's personal experience in the shop and mentions repairs only briefly.
No, because it argues that teenagers should not work during the summer.
questions.e: The essay is a personal story about one summer; repairs appear only as part of that story, and most are just named, not explained. A and B treat small details as the main purpose. D is false — the essay argues nothing of the kind.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Match the exact goal words — not just a true, nice sentence.
"Specific" = numbers, names, exact places; "picture" = a concrete image.
Two-part goals need both parts.
"Suppose…": compare topic, kind of essay and scope with what the essay really does; then check the reason is true.
A detail mentioned once is never the essay's primary purpose.
